Begin with the reader's job

A good content brief tells a writer who needs the piece and what that person should be able to do after reading it. Give Maia the audience notes, the search or campaign intent, the publishing format, and the next action you want the reader to take. Include the editorial rules that affect length, voice, links, and review.

Avoid starting with a broad topic alone. "Write about campaign reporting" leaves the key choices open. "Help a marketing manager prepare a weekly paid-campaign review without misreading an incomplete attribution window" gives the brief a real job.

Ground the outline in sources

Supply the research that the writer is allowed to use. This may include interview notes, approved product material, public references, and a current editorial plan. Ask Maia to attach sources to factual claims and mark unsupported ideas as questions or proposed angles.

The distinction matters when the source material mixes facts with opinions. A customer interview can support what that person experienced, but it does not prove that every team has the same problem. The brief should preserve that boundary for the writer.

Make choices before drafting

The brief should settle the page's promise, scope, and structure. It can name the opening situation, the sections needed to answer the reader's question, examples worth developing, and claims that require a subject matter review. It should also state what the piece will leave out.

Suppose the supplied research contains three definitions of an active customer. Maia should not pick one because it appears most often. The brief can display the conflict, explain which planned section depends on it, and ask the editor to choose the approved definition.

Give the writer room to write

A brief is a set of decisions, not a first draft broken into bullets. Keep boilerplate out of the output. Ask for concrete source notes and editorial direction where they change the work. Let the writer choose transitions and phrasing.

Review the brief in Slack with the writer and the subject matter owner. They can correct the audience, reject a weak angle, or add a missing source in the same thread. Maia can update the assignment after those decisions.

Try one real assignment

Choose a piece already on the calendar and collect its approved inputs. Ask Maia for the brief, then check every source link and proposed claim. Have the assigned writer mark anything that remains ambiguous. Save the corrected structure as reusable guidance only if it applies to future work.

Questions from content teams

Can Maia do the research too?

Maia can work with public sources and connected apps it is allowed to access. Name the research question and required source types. An editor should check recency, identity, and whether each source supports the claim.

How does Maia handle an unsupported product claim?

Ask it to label the claim as proposed and add the evidence needed. The claim should stay out of the draft until the product owner approves support for it.

Can we reuse one brief for several formats?

Use the approved facts and audience decision as shared inputs, then create a separate assignment for each format. A webinar outline and a search page have different constraints even when they begin with the same research.
